blocks.x: They took it out and did what with it?
They added to it and sent it to your dependent. © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

Well they added to it with quarters and subsistence I think it amounted to around oh I think around $87 or $92 a month or something like that. But see in 1942 for crying out loud, what was the rent? People were paying — oh heck they weren’t paying very much rent. Because you had price and wage controls. So that was to prevent gouging. And so I think I was living with my in-laws but then when I got the apartment I think it was — was it $27.50 a month? Something like that. For a one bedroom duplex. So anyhow we lived off the base. And the fellas that had cars, they would have carpools. And since they had to use the car to get to and from work why they could get gas coupons. So what happened, Marshall started organizing the band, putting the band together. And for me, boy, it was really something. Because I had never been in company that fast before. So gradually I came around, you know, gradually. I started taking lessons from Herb Sanford, he was one of my teachers. He was an old Vaudevillian and played in the dime dances, oh yeah, and he played percussion. He played marimba and the vibraphone as well. And so anyhow over a period of time the band shaped up. And we would, besides playing a dance every Sunday for the cadets, see the USO would bring hostesses out and they’d recruit them from the universities and from the different servicemens’ associations. They would recruit the young ladies and they would come out to the base and they had a huge drill hall with a beautiful wooden floor and they had a bandstand there and we would play every Sunday for dances for the cadets. Then we would record once a week for the OWI, Office of War Information, and they would set up a telephone and we’d do a remote, and we were remote, and then the recording would take place in the city. And then you could come over here to an office they had down on Sutter and Kearney and you could go upstairs and listen to the playback. And these records, they would be broadcast overseas to the Twelfth Naval District.

They weren’t really V-disks, because I think the V-disks were smaller. These were large glass. They ended up large glass disks, and we would go down there. We recorded two for another — what was it, the Office of War Information and something else, someone else we recorded for. So we could have done V-disks because they were very popular. I know I think the Glenn Miller overseas band I think they did V-disks, and so many of the other service bands. But with us it turned out that we were considered as a top rated band in the Twelfth Naval District, which was a great honor. Because here you had — Artie Shaw was in the South Pacific, he had a band, and when he got out Sam Donahue took it over. And Davy Tough was in that band and it was all full of Los Angeles studio musicians. Then the Coast Guard here had an excellent band. Then Pete Rugulo was in an Army band, they had an Army band and Pete Rugulo was their arranger, and where else? © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-
